title: Friday
subtitle: The Thirty-First: a Viaduct at Noon, a Rally at Eight, a Shot at 8:40, a Train at 10:40

setting.name: Port Calloway, Friday 31 October 1952, Halloween, the fifth anniversary of the execution of Daniel Kessling
setting.description: The last day of the clock. By now the party should know who means to kill Wendell Sloane, where and when, and why; and Friday is the day they decide what to do about it. The morning belongs to the bomb (found at seven by Dunleavy, or the night before by the party), to Gil Maddox's arrest, and to Sloane's grand jury, which reports at ten. At noon the Shoreline Viaduct is dedicated over the Tin Mile, with Sloane, the mayor and the governor's highway commissioner on a bunting-hung platform above Pier 9 and the ruin of the Halvorsen Cannery. In the afternoon the city gets ready for Halloween and the election, and the party gets ready for the Regent. At eight the Regent's doors open for Sloane's election-eve rally, broadcast live on radio station KCAL; at 8:40 he speaks; at 8:40 Ansel Teague means to shoot him from Box A as Nora Kessling stands up in the balcony; at 10:40 Constance Sloane's train leaves for the south. Whatever happens, at midnight the Courier's late edition goes to press, and the Ledger's Saturday edition at two.
setting.atmosphere: Rain, harder than all week, and a wind off the sound that turns umbrellas inside out. Halloween: children in sheets and paper masks on the Tin Mile, jack-o'-lanterns in windows on Larch Hill, a bonfire on the beach below the Flats. Election bunting soaked and sagging. The viaduct dedication: a brass band from the high school, the governor's man in a homburg, a ribbon, a crowd of Tin Mile people watching from under the concrete legs, and the black ruin of Pier 9 below the platform where nobody looks. The Regent: two thousand people, wet coats, red plush, a radio microphone on the lectern, flashbulbs, a band playing 'Happy Days Are Here Again' until someone remembers it is the other party's song. Run the last act in something close to real time. Say the time aloud. Let the clock on the Regent's proscenium arch be a character.

keyLocations.name: The Hall of Justice and the DA's Office, Friday Morning
keyLocations.description: Sloane's third-floor office at nine, an hour before the grand jury reports. Agnes Ruud at her desk, Dunleavy in the corridor glowing with having 'found' a bomb, reporters from both papers on the stairs, Maddox in a cell in the basement. Sloane has summoned the party to collect what he paid for.
features: Sloane's office: flags, law books, a window onto Commerce Street, the Regent across the way with its marquee: TONIGHT: SLOANE FOR DA
The grand jury room down the corridor, where at ten the waterfront report is read and two of Maddox's lieutenants are indicted
The holding cells in the basement, where Gil Maddox, arrested at eight, is calling for his lawyer and for Sloane's head
encounters: Wendell Sloane, who wants a name and the paper, and offers $5,000 for both
Lt. Dunleavy, the morning's hero, with his photograph in the Courier's noon edition
Gil Maddox in a basement cell, who will talk to the party if they come down
secrets: Sloane, at nine, is at his most dangerous: he thinks the bomb was the threat and it is over. He asks the party for 'whatever paper the Kessling girl has' and a written report, and says the rest of the fee is now $5,000, not $500, 'for your discretion'. If the party tells him the truth (Teague, Vantreight, Box A), he goes white, then calculates: he wants Teague stopped, Vantreight ruined, Nora arrested anyway and the paper burned. He will not cancel the rally: 'If I hide on election eve, I lose, and if I lose, I'm dead anyway.'

If the party confronts Sloane with the fire (the original statement, Lindqvist, Lusk, the carbon), he does not deny it. He says, 'Eleven people died and a man was executed and I made a career of it. Now. What do you want?' He offers anything: money, a job, a pardon for Nora if she is charged, the original burned and the party rich. He also says, truthfully, that if he dies tonight Vantreight wins everything. That is the campaign's hardest argument and the players must answer it themselves.

Gil Maddox, in his cell, has worked out that Dorrance sold him. If the party tells him who to, he will say on the record that he paid Sloane $500 a month for six years and that Dorrance reported to Dunleavy. He would very much like to watch Larch Hill burn.

keyLocations.name: The Shoreline Viaduct, Noon
keyLocations.description: The dedication of the first finished mile of the viaduct, on the upper deck above Pier 9: a bunting-hung platform, a ribbon, folding chairs for dignitaries, the high-school band, the governor's highway commissioner, the mayor, Sloane, and a crowd of two or three hundred on the lower deck and in the street beneath. Directly below the platform: the black ruin of the Halvorsen Cannery, scheduled for demolition in December.
features: The platform: the mayor, the commissioner, Sloane, a microphone, a pair of golden scissors
The crowd under the concrete legs: Tin Mile people who have lost their homes to the right-of-way, cannery women, Local 9 men, children skipping school for Halloween
The view from the platform rail: straight down onto Pier 9, the wire fence and the wreaths
encounters: Sloane, the mayor, the highway commissioner, Special Agent Warren Hale of the FBI (watching, on the freeway-fraud detail)
Nora Kessling, in the crowd at the fence, if she is not with the party
Mrs. Hedda Sorvik with her candle, and Frank Lusk, alone, at the back of the crowd
Teague, on the lower deck, watching Sloane through the rain, not working, just looking
secrets: This scene is a mood scene and a chance. Nothing is planned to happen here; the bomb has been found. But a party that has the original statement and Lusk can make something happen: Lusk, if the party has broken him, can walk up to the microphone after Sloane cuts the ribbon and say, in front of the commissioner, the FBI and the newspapers, what he did in 1947. It is the bravest thing he will ever do, and it changes the night: Sloane is ruined by suppertime and Vantreight's frame no longer makes sense. Teague, watching, takes a long look at the party and decides to finish the job anyway, because he has been paid.

Special Agent Warren Hale is in Port Calloway because the Bureau of Public Roads has asked the Justice Department about the viaduct land awards. He has the Northgate fraud complaint the DA's office buried. He is the party's route around Vantreight's police and courts: give him the E3 records, the money bands and the carbon, and he can freeze the Northgate awards by Monday; give him Teague or the Courier proof, and he can arrest Dunleavy tonight for a federal conspiracy.

keyLocations.name: The Regent Theatre, Friday Night
keyLocations.description: Two thousand seats, full. The rally runs: 8:00 doors, band, balloons; 8:15 the KCAL radio broadcast begins; 8:20 the mayor; 8:30 a Local 9 vice-president's endorsement (Lusk was to give it and has not been seen); 8:40 Sloane at the lectern; 9:15 Sloane finishes; 9:30 the house empties. Box A stage left is empty on the plan and reserved 'for the DA's guests'. Seat C-14 in the front of the balcony is Nora's complimentary ticket.
features: The lectern at stage centre, with the KCAL microphone and a glass of water
Box A, lower tier stage left, behind a velvet curtain, eleven yards from the lectern, reached by a pass door from backstage
The fly gallery over the stage-left wings, the iron stair down to the alley door, Pop Kinsella's cubbyhole
The balcony front row, C-14, a clear line from Box A
The projection booth at the back of the balcony, unused tonight, with a window over the whole house: Teague's second route
The clock on the proscenium arch, gilt, four feet across, always two minutes slow
encounters: Sloane at the lectern
Ansel Teague (The Professional), in Box A by 8:35 (or in the projection booth, second route)
Lt. Dunleavy (Bent Detective) and two of his men (Crooked Cop) backstage
Becerra and the honest cops on the front doors, unless the party has moved them
Nora Kessling in C-14, or wherever the party has persuaded her to be
Constance Sloane, in the front row of the orchestra, on the aisle, with her handbag on her knee
secrets: THE PLAN (if nobody has changed it): 8:35 Teague enters Box A through the pass door with a Colt .32 and sits behind the curtain. At about 8:40, as Sloane says the words 'five years ago this very night', which are in his prepared speech because his speechwriter does not know what they mean, Nora stands up in C-14 with her photostat and shouts 'Tell them about Pier 9!', and every head turns to the balcony. Teague fires twice at Sloane from the box, eleven yards, in the uproar, and is through the pass door, along the fly gallery and out of the alley door in two minutes ten. Dunleavy's two men are on the balcony stairs in thirty seconds, Dunleavy takes Nora's .32 from her handbag, puts Teague's twin, fired once that afternoon into a sandbag, in its place, and arrests her in front of two thousand witnesses who saw her stand up and shout. The Courier's late edition prints.

THE SECOND ROUTE (if Teague knows he was seen on Thursday): he does not use Box A. He is in the projection booth at the back of the balcony, behind C-14, from 8:00, and fires over Nora's head as she stands, so that the shots come from where she is. The frame works better. Spotting him: Perception DC 15 from the stage or the orchestra, or anyone who checks the booth (the door is locked; Pop Kinsella has the key and gave Teague a copy for $20 more).

Dunleavy does not know Teague might use the second route; Teague does not trust him. If the party arrests or occupies Dunleavy first, Teague goes ahead anyway; if the party gets Teague first, Dunleavy has no gun to swap and no story, and tries to arrest the party instead.
Constance's handbag holds the original 1946 statement if she has not given it away. She has come to watch, because she wants to see him one more time, and she has a train at 10:40.

keyLocations.name: Union Station and the Ledger, Late
keyLocations.description: Union Station, a granite barn by the freight yards, where the 10:40 Coast Daylight Connection leaves for the south from track 4. The Ledger Building, where Hollis Gage holds the Saturday front page open until two in the morning, and Nora Kessling's switchboard is dark for the first night in five years.
features: Track 4, the 10:40 south, steam and porters and the station clock
Hollis Gage's office, his lawyer, his safe, his cold coffee and the Saturday page waiting for its lead
The Ledger presses in the basement, which start at two
encounters: Constance Sloane on track 4, if she has not changed her plans
Hollis Gage and his lawyer, Morton Frye, deciding what can be printed
Ansel Teague on the 11:15 to Portland, if he got away
secrets: What the Ledger can print depends on what the party gives Gage. A dead watchman's photostat alone: no. The original 1946 statement with Constance's sworn word that she typed it, or Lindqvist's fresh witnessed statement, or Lusk's signed confession: yes. Any two of those, plus the Hall of Records figures: THE HALVORSEN FIRE: DA BURIED WITNESS; VANTREIGHT MANAGER PAID WATCHMAN across eight columns. Add the Courier proof and Teague, and Gage prints the story of the century and dares Vantreight to sue.

Teague, if he got away, is on the 11:15 to Portland with the second half of his fee due on Saturday. Special Agent Hale can have him taken off the train at the state line if the party gives Hale enough by eleven. If no one does, he is gone, and the party will think about him for the rest of their lives.

synopsis: Friday is the reckoning. At seven Lt. Dunleavy finds the bomb under the DA's Packard (if the party has not already stopped it) and is a hero in the noon Courier; Gil Maddox is arrested by eight and knows he was sold. At nine Sloane summons the party to collect his paper and offers $5,000 for it; the party can lie to him, tell him everything, or confront him with the fire. At ten his grand jury reports. At noon the viaduct is dedicated over the ruin of Pier 9, and Frank Lusk, if the party has broken him, can tell the truth at the microphone. In the afternoon the party makes its plan for the Regent with whoever they have won to their side: Becerra and the honest cops, the FBI's Special Agent Hale, Nora, Constance, Hollis Gage, even Maddox. At 8:40 that night, if nothing has been changed, Ansel Teague shoots Wendell Sloane from Box A as Nora stands up in the balcony, and Dunleavy swaps her gun for Teague's twin and arrests her in front of two thousand people. The party can stop Teague in the box or the projection booth, stop Dunleavy's swap, get Nora out of the balcony or keep her there with the photostat and a microphone, let Sloane die, or save him to face the truth. At 10:40 Constance's train leaves. At two in the morning the Ledger goes to press with whatever the party has given it. The ending is the players' choice: who lives, who is blamed, who pays, and whether the truth about the Halvorsen fire makes the front page.
hook: Friday, 6:55 a.m. The phone in the agency office again, and this time it is Agnes Ruud, whispering from the third floor of the Hall of Justice. They've found a bomb under Mr. Sloane's car, she says. Lieutenant Dunleavy found it. There are photographers. Mr. Sloane wants you in his office at nine. He says, she says, and her voice breaks a little, he says to tell you it's all over and you can bring him what he paid for.

conclusions.conclusion: H. The attempt is at the Regent at 8:40
clues: H1: the seating plan (the Meridian, Thursday)
H2: Pop Kinsella (the Regent stage door)
H3: the security rota (Becerra or Agnes Ruud)
The marquee and Sloane's prepared speech text, which Agnes typed: 'five years ago this very night' at the 8:40 mark
Frank Lusk's confession, signed or said at the viaduct microphone
The Hall of Records figures (E3) and the Northgate bands (B1, E5)
Her own .32, unfired, in Dunleavy's pocket if he made the swap

acts.title: Act 1: The Hero of the Hour
acts.description: Friday morning, seven to noon. The bomb has been found and the city thinks the danger is over. The party knows better. Sloane's nine o'clock meeting is the campaign's last conversation with the client and its sharpest: what do they tell him? Then the party gathers its allies and its evidence and makes a plan. Make them say the plan out loud.
objectives: Decide what to tell Sloane, and what to give him
Decide whether to try to stop the rally, or use it
Gather allies: Becerra, Special Agent Hale, Hollis Gage, Nora, Constance, Lusk, even Maddox
Put the evidence somewhere safe, in more than one place

scenes.name: What He Paid For
scenes.description: Sloane's office at nine. He is triumphant, shaved, smelling of bay rum, with the Courier's early edition on his desk: DA BOMB PLOT FOILED. He wants a written report, the Kessling girl's paper, and the party's discretion until Tuesday, for $5,000. He does not believe there is anything more coming. What the party says here sets up the night.
scenes.readAloud: He is standing at the window with his hands in his pockets, looking across Commerce Street at the Regent's marquee, where a man on a ladder in the rain is putting up the letters of his name. On his desk, the Courier, still damp from the press, with a photograph of Ray Dunleavy holding up a bundle of dynamite like a prize salmon. 'Well,' says Wendell Sloane, turning, and he is smiling the poster smile, and for the first time all week it almost reaches his eyes. 'Maddox. Gil Maddox, of all the tin-pot hoodlums. I hired you to tell me who and the police told me first.' He sits, and takes out a chequebook, and uncaps a fountain pen. 'Never mind. I'm a fair man. You'll give me your report, and whatever that girl at the Ledger's been carrying round, and you'll forget all about it till after Tuesday, and I'll make this out for five thousand dollars.' He looks up. 'That's ten times what we agreed. I'd call that generous.'

skillChecks.success: Sloane believes whatever story the party tells him: that Nora has nothing, that the paper was burned, that the job is done. He writes the cheque (on a Northgate account, of course) and goes to the rally believing he is safe, which means he will stand at the lectern exactly as planned. The party now has total control of the evening, and total responsibility.
skillChecks.failure: Sloane knows they are lying. He says nothing, writes nothing, and when they leave he telephones Dunleavy: the party is to be kept out of the Regent tonight. Dunleavy's men are on every door. Getting in now needs a ticket and a disguise (Deception DC 14), Becerra, Pop Kinsella, or the Ledger's press seats.

skillChecks.success: If the party tells Sloane the truth about Teague and Vantreight: he believes them, because it is exactly what he would do. He will let the party (and Becerra) handle Box A, and will not cancel. He will also, privately, ask the party to make sure Nora is arrested anyway, and that the original statement 'finds its way to my safe'. Insight DC 12: if Sloane survives tonight, he will try to destroy everyone who knows, including the party.
skillChecks.failure: Sloane does not believe them, or pretends not to. 'Vantreight? Cornelius made me. He's my oldest friend in this city.' He laughs. His hand is shaking. He goes to the rally anyway.

skillChecks.success: If the party confronts him with the fire and the evidence: he stops pretending, and offers them anything to bury it. And then, pushed past the offer, he says the one honest thing he has left: 'If I die tonight, Cornelius gets the viaduct and the girl gets the gas chamber, like her father. If I live, I lose on Tuesday and I go to prison. Those are the choices. You pick.' The party now knows he will not save himself by confessing. +1 Heat.
skillChecks.failure: Sloane calls for Dunleavy and has the party shown out of the Hall of Justice. +1 Heat. They are not welcome at the Regent.

scenes.name: Friends in Low Places
scenes.description: The morning's other conversations, in whatever order the party chooses, a scene each: Becerra (the rota, the honest cops; he can put himself and two men backstage if the party gives him a reason his captain will accept), Special Agent Warren Hale at the Federal Building (needs evidence of federal fraud or a conspiracy across state lines: Teague's Portland ticket and the Northgate checks will do), Hollis Gage at the Ledger (what he will print, and when), Nora (what she plans; whether she will go to the rally), Constance (whether she will give up the original, and to whom), Frank Lusk (whether he will speak at the viaduct), and Gil Maddox in his cell (testimony against Dunleavy and Sloane, for a deal).
scenes.readAloud: Special Agent Warren Hale's office is a borrowed room on the fourth floor of the Federal Building, a desk, two chairs, a filing cabinet and a calendar from a Spokane feed store, and Hale is a lean grey Kansan in a grey suit with a crew cut and a wedding ring, reading the Northgate fraud complaint for the third time with a pencil. He listens to all of it without interrupting, and then he takes off his glasses and says, 'Private detectives, a dead watchman, a pawnbroker, a newspaper page that hasn't been printed yet, and the richest man in the state.' He puts his glasses back on. 'Show me the train ticket again.'

skillChecks.success: Hale is in. With Teague's interstate ticket, the Northgate cashier's checks and the buried federal-highway fraud complaint, he has the start of a federal conspiracy case, and enough to act tonight. He will be at the Regent with two agents, in the balcony, and will arrest Teague if the party points him out, and Dunleavy if Becerra will swear a complaint.
skillChecks.failure: Hale is interested but cannot act on a theory. He will be at the Regent, alone, watching. If something happens in front of him, he will act.

skillChecks.success: Nora: she is going to the rally whatever anyone says, and she will stand up at 8:40, because it is the anniversary and because she promised her father's grave. But she will leave the gun at home if someone she trusts asks her to, and will sit in a different seat if the party explains the frame (and is visibly shaken to learn that she was the bait). She would rather read the statement into the KCAL microphone than shout it from the balcony, if the party can get her to the stage.
skillChecks.failure: Nora says she is going, and that what she does is her business. She takes the gun.

skillChecks.success: Hollis Gage: 'Give me the original, or a living witness, or Lusk on paper, by midnight, and the Ledger leads with it at two o'clock. Give me all three and I'll print it in red.' He offers the party two press seats in the orchestra pit, with Iris Nakamura and her camera.
skillChecks.failure: Gage is cagey; his lawyer has frightened him. He wants the evidence first and promises nothing.

encounters: Dunleavy (Bent Detective) in the Hall of Justice corridor, all smiles, telling the party they can go home now
No combat expected in this act.

acts.title: Act 2: A Ribbon over Pier 9
acts.description: Noon to evening. The viaduct dedication (a mood scene and a chance for Lusk), then the afternoon of preparation. Teague checks out of the Meridian at two (or has already, if spooked) and leaves a suitcase at Union Station's left luggage. The party can try to take him before the rally: he is at the Meridian grill at one, at the station at two, at a cinema on Commerce Street from three to seven (he likes to sit in the dark before a job), and at the Regent's alley door at 7:45.
objectives: Be at the viaduct dedication, and decide whether anyone speaks
Take Teague before the rally, or decide to take him at the Regent
Get the party (and allies) into the Regent and into position
Decide where Nora will be at 8:40

scenes.name: The Ribbon
scenes.description: Noon on the viaduct's upper deck. The ceremony runs fifteen minutes: the band, the mayor, the commissioner, Sloane cutting the ribbon with golden scissors and saying 'progress' four times. Below the platform, Pier 9. If Lusk has been broken, he walks to the microphone afterwards. If not, nothing happens except that Sloane, looking down for a photograph, sees the wreaths on the Halvorsen fence and for one second forgets to smile.
scenes.readAloud: The upper deck of the viaduct is a grey concrete road in the sky, slick with rain, running away north into fog, and on it a platform hung with wet bunting, a ribbon, a brass band of shivering schoolboys, and twenty men in homburgs. Below, on the lower deck and under the concrete legs and in the street, a few hundred people from the Tin Mile have come to watch the road that took their homes being opened: cannery women in headscarves, longshoremen, children in paper masks for Halloween. Wendell Sloane takes the golden scissors from the mayor and smiles for the cameras and leans out over the rail for the photographers below, and for a moment, looking straight down, he is looking at the black wall of the Halvorsen Cannery and the wreaths on its fence, and his smile goes out like a light. Then the flashbulbs pop, and he cuts the ribbon, and the band plays.

skillChecks.success: Frank Lusk, if the party has his confession (E4) or has shown him the statement: he walks to the microphone after the ribbon, before anyone can stop him, and says, into the rain, in front of the commissioner and the FBI and both newspapers, that he lied at Danny Kessling's trial in 1947 because the district attorney's office dropped a charge against him, and that he is sorry. It takes a minute. The crowd under the viaduct is silent, and then Mrs. Sorvik begins to clap. Sloane is finished by suppertime. Teague, on the lower deck, looks at the party and decides to complete the job anyway.
skillChecks.failure: Lusk comes to the viaduct and stands at the back and cannot do it. He leaves. He will sign a statement for Hollis Gage tonight if someone goes with him.

skillChecks.success: On the lower deck, at the rail, a grey coat and a grey hat, a man watching Sloane, not the ceremony. He is not working. He is looking. He turns his head and sees you, and touches his hat brim, very slightly, and walks away into the crowd.
skillChecks.failure: You do not see Teague in the crowd. He sees you.

scenes.name: Before the Doors
scenes.description: The afternoon. Taking Teague early is possible and dangerous: in the cinema on Commerce Street, in the dark, between three and seven (a tail from the Meridian or the station finds him); at Union Station's left-luggage counter at two. He is The Professional and will kill to get away; in a cinema he has a .32, a straight razor, and two hundred people to hide among. Taken alive, he never speaks without a federal deal, and Hale can offer one. Otherwise: getting into the Regent (Becerra, Pop Kinsella, Gage's press seats, tickets and disguises), positioning allies (Box A, the fly gallery, the projection booth, the balcony stairs), and Nora.
scenes.readAloud: By five the rain is coming sideways off the sound and the Regent's marquee is lit, SLOANE FOR DA, TONIGHT 8 PM, BROADCAST ON KCAL, the bulbs running round its edge in a chase that never catches up. Across the street, in the Meridian lobby, men in wet coats are reading newspapers with your client's face on them. At the stage door in Pike Alley, Pop Kinsella is sitting in his cubbyhole with a pint of rye and a radio, and he looks up when you come down the alley, and says, 'Busy night, for a fire survey.'

skillChecks.success: If the party goes for Teague in the cinema: you are in the row behind him before he knows. The fight is in the dark, in seconds, and the party has surprise; a knockout blow with a blackjack or nightstick from surprise forces a CON save. Taken, he says only, 'I should like to speak to a federal officer.'
skillChecks.failure: He knows you are there. He leaves by the fire exit during the newsreel and is not seen again until the Regent, on his second route.

skillChecks.success: Pop Kinsella, for another pint and the truth, gives you the stage-door key, the pass-door key to Box A, and, frowning, mentions that the insurance fella paid him another $20 on Thursday night for a copy of the projection-booth key. The second route.
skillChecks.failure: Pop lets you in by the stage door. He does not mention the projection booth unless asked.

encounters: The viaduct: no combat. Teague in the crowd, watching.
Teague (The Professional) if the party goes for him early, in the cinema or at the station: he fights only to escape, and he fights very well
Dunleavy's men (2 Crooked Cop) on the Regent's doors if Sloane has told Dunleavy to keep the party out

acts.title: Act 3: Eight-Forty
acts.description: The Regent, 8:00 to 9:30, run as close to real time as the table can bear. The clock on the proscenium arch is always two minutes slow. Then Union Station at 10:40 and the Ledger at two. Every outcome depends on what the party set up; run the plan, then run the people who do not know about the plan. This is the campaign's finale, and its question is not whether the party is clever enough to save Sloane, but whether they want to, and at what price.
objectives: Stop Teague, or let him shoot
Stop Dunleavy's gun swap, or prove it
Keep Nora out of the frame, and decide whether she speaks
Get the truth to someone who can print it or act on it by midnight
Settle accounts: Sloane, Vantreight, Dunleavy, Teague, Constance, Nora

scenes.name: The House Lights
scenes.description: 8:00 to 8:40. The doors, the band, the radio broadcast at 8:15, the mayor at 8:20, the endorsements, Sloane in the wings, Dunleavy backstage, Teague arriving at the pass door at 8:35 (or already in the projection booth since 8:00), Nora in C-14 or wherever she has agreed to be, Constance on the orchestra aisle. Let the players move their pieces; describe what each of them sees at each minute.
scenes.readAloud: Two thousand people in wet coats, steam rising off them under the chandeliers, the band playing 'Happy Days Are Here Again' until someone in a homburg hisses at the conductor and they switch to a Sousa march. Balloons. Placards on sticks: SLOANE KEEPS CALLOWAY SAFE. A KCAL announcer in a booth by the pit is saying the time into a microphone. The gilt clock on the proscenium arch says 8:31, which means it is 8:33. Behind the velvet curtain of Box A, stage left, nothing moves. In the front row of the balcony, a dark-haired young woman sits with a cardboard folder on her knees and her handbag on top of it, and does not take her eyes off the lectern. In the wings, a tall man in a navy suit straightens his tie in a fire bucket's reflection, and a big red-faced man beside him moves a toothpick from one side of his mouth to the other, and looks at his watch.

skillChecks.success: At 8:35 the curtain of Box A moves, a hand's width, and is still. Or, on the second route: in the projection booth's little square window at the back of the balcony, where no light should be, the red point of a cigarette, and then not. You know where he is.
skillChecks.failure: You see nothing in the box or the booth. Your allies may have: ask them.

skillChecks.success: Through the pass door or up the balcony back stair to the booth without Dunleavy's men or Teague seeing you. You reach him with seconds to spare, before 8:40, from behind. Fight in a velvet box or a tin booth, with two thousand people singing below; the band covers the first ten seconds of anything.
skillChecks.failure: One of Dunleavy's men is on the pass door (or the booth stair) and asks your business. Talk past him (Deception DC 13, The Badge, Becerra), or put him down quietly (a knockout blow from surprise is no longer possible; a grapple and a blackjack might be). Every round costs a minute on the clock.

scenes.name: Five Years Ago This Very Night
scenes.description: 8:40. Sloane at the lectern, the speech, the line, and whatever the party has arranged. Possibilities: Teague taken before he fires; Teague fires and someone shields Sloane, or spoils the shot (a thrown chair, a shout, Becerra in the box); Nora stands up and reads the statement into a balcony full of people (or, if the party has arranged it, walks onto the stage and reads it into the KCAL microphone, which Sloane cannot stop without looking like what he is); Dunleavy goes for Nora and finds the party or Hale in the way; Constance stands up in the orchestra with the original in her hand. Or nobody does anything and Sloane dies.
scenes.readAloud: 'My friends,' says Wendell Sloane into the microphone, and two thousand people go quiet, and the rain drums on the Regent's roof like a crowd that could not get in. 'Five years ago this very night,' and he stops, because he has just heard what he is saying, and the house waits, and in the front row of the balcony a young woman stands up with a folder in her hands, and in the silence her voice carries to every seat in the house: 'Tell them about Pier 9!' Two thousand heads turn to the balcony. Wendell Sloane's face, under the lights, has gone the colour of the paper in her hands. Behind the velvet curtain of Box A, eleven yards from the lectern, a gloved hand draws the curtain back an inch.

skillChecks.success: You are between Sloane and the box (or the booth), or you have hit Sloane at the knees and taken him to the floor behind the lectern, or you have put your shoulder into Teague as he aims. The first shot goes into the proscenium arch and stops the clock at 8:38. Roll initiative for everything after.
skillChecks.failure: Teague fires. Sloane is hit once (the GM decides: wounded, or dead). The second shot misses because someone shouted. The house erupts. Roll initiative.

skillChecks.success: In the balcony uproar, before Dunleavy's men reach her, you take Nora's .32 out of her handbag and pass it to Hale, Becerra, Iris Nakamura or Gage, in front of a witness. When Dunleavy arrives with his twin gun there is nothing to swap and a press camera in his face. His frame is dead.
skillChecks.failure: Dunleavy's man gets to Nora first and has her handbag. The swap happens unless someone stops Dunleavy physically or Iris photographs it (Perception DC 13 for her to be looking the right way).

skillChecks.success: Nora, or a party member, or Constance, reaches the lectern or the KCAL microphone and reads the Lindqvist statement aloud, every word, to two thousand people in the theatre and fifty thousand on the radio. Sloane does not stop them. He sits down on the edge of the stage and listens, like a man hearing his own sentence. Nothing that happens afterwards can make it unsaid.
skillChecks.failure: The microphone is cut by the KCAL engineer, on Dunleavy's order. The theatre heard it; the radio did not. The Ledger will have to do the rest.

scenes.name: The 10:40 and the Two O'Clock Edition
scenes.description: Afterwards. Union Station: Constance on track 4, with or without the original; Teague on the 11:15 if he got away, and Hale's call to the state line. The Ledger: Hollis Gage, his lawyer and the page, and what the party can put in front of them by midnight. Sloane: alive and ruined, alive and dangerous, or dead. Vantreight: listening to KCAL at Greyholme with a glass of brandy, and what he hears. Close the campaign with Saturday morning's two front pages, read aloud, and Sloane's second $500, which arrives at the agency on Saturday in an envelope, if he is alive to send it, with a note that says only: Paid in full.
scenes.readAloud: Union Station at twenty to eleven is a granite barn full of steam and echoes, porters, sailors on leave, a family asleep on a bench with their suitcases tied with string. Track 4. The train south is breathing at the platform, its windows lit, and halfway along it a slim fair woman in a grey travelling coat is standing by an open door with a small suitcase, not getting on. The station clock says 10:38. She sees you coming down the platform, and she does not move, and when you reach her she opens her handbag and takes out a long envelope, yellowed, soft at the folds, and holds it for a moment against her coat. 'I typed it,' Constance Sloane says. 'I gave him a glass of water. Eleven people.' The conductor calls the train. She holds the envelope out to you. 'Somebody ought to get to keep something,' she says, 'from all this.'

skillChecks.success: Constance gives the original to the party (or to Nora, or to Gage) and gets on the train, or does not get on the train and goes with the party to the Ledger to swear to it. Either is a good ending for her.
skillChecks.failure: Constance gets on the train with the envelope and mails it to Miriam Holloway from Salem. It arrives on Monday, a day before the election. Holloway uses it. It is enough, just.

skillChecks.success: At the Ledger by midnight, with enough evidence (see the Union Station and Ledger key location), Hollis Gage's lawyer says yes, and Gage takes the page down to the composing room himself. The Ledger's Saturday headline is the party's to write.
skillChecks.failure: Gage's lawyer says no to something the party wanted printed, and is right to: it is not proved. The story runs, smaller. Vantreight's lawyers are on the phone by nine.

encounters: Ansel Teague (The Professional), Box A or the projection booth, with a Colt .32 pocket pistol and a straight razor. He fights to escape, not to win; he will cut his way through anyone between him and the alley door or the balcony back stair. Captured alive, he asks for a federal officer and says nothing else.

Lt. Ray Dunleavy (Bent Detective) and 2 Crooked Cops backstage and on the balcony stairs. Dunleavy will not fire on the party in front of two thousand witnesses unless he thinks he can call it self-defence; his men will, if he tells them to. If his frame collapses, he tries to arrest the party, then to leave by the alley, then to make a deal.
Becerra and up to four honest Beat Cops on the front doors; Special Agent Warren Hale (Federal Agent) and, if persuaded, two more Federal Agents in the balcony
Two thousand panicking people: any fight in the house is in difficult terrain, and any missed shot has a chance (the GM's call, 1 in 6) of hitting a bystander; +3 Heat if one is hit

npcsInvolved.name: Wendell Sloane, 52
npcsInvolved.role: The client; the target; the man who buried the truth
npcsInvolved.description: Shaved, bay rum, the poster smile, a speech with a line in it he has not read carefully enough. Tonight he is braver than he has ever been, because he cannot afford not to be, and more dangerous, because he is cornered.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To survive tonight and win on Tuesday. If he cannot have both, the first. If he survives and is ruined, revenge on everyone who knew.

npcsInvolved.name: Ansel Teague, about 45
npcsInvolved.description: As before. Tonight he wears a dark suit instead of the grey coat, and gloves. He does not hate Sloane. He does not think about him at all.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Two shots, two minutes ten, the 11:15 to Portland, the second half of the fee, and the last hundred pages of The Way We Live Now.

npcsInvolved.name: Lt. Ray Dunleavy, 48
npcsInvolved.description: As before, in his best suit, with Nora's twin in his coat pocket and a photographer from the Courier told to stand by the balcony stairs at 8:41.

npcsInvolved.name: Nora Kessling, 26
npcsInvolved.role: The bait, the witness, the daughter
npcsInvolved.description: Full sheet in the companion files. Tonight, whatever the party has told her, she is going to stand up. The only questions are where, with what in her hands, and who is standing beside her.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Her father's name, said out loud, cleared, tonight.

npcsInvolved.name: Constance Sloane, 44
npcsInvolved.description: In the orchestra on the aisle in black, then on track 4 in grey. Has come to see her husband one last time. Will stand up, if Nora does and no one else will.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To give the envelope to someone who will do something with it, and get on a train.

npcsInvolved.name: Special Agent Warren Hale, 44
npcsInvolved.role: FBI, freeway-fraud detail; the outside authority
npcsInvolved.description: A lean, grey, patient Kansan, Methodist, crew cut, wedding ring, no sense of humour about corruption. Use Federal Agent. The one man in Port Calloway whom Vantreight does not own, because he does not live there.
npcsInvolved.motivation: A clean case that will stand up in a federal court in Seattle, and the 7:15 train home to his family on Sunday.

npcsInvolved.name: Hollis Gage, 61
npcsInvolved.description: Small, bald, bow tie, ink on his cuffs, owes money to everyone and fears no one. Has spent twenty years losing a newspaper war to Vantreight and enjoyed every minute of it.
npcsInvolved.motivation: One great front page before the Ledger goes broke. And beating the Courier to it.

npcsInvolved.name: Cornelius Vantreight, 67
npcsInvolved.description: Never leaves Greyholme tonight. Listens to KCAL in the library with a glass of brandy and the viaduct model at his elbow. If the party wants to confront him, it will have to be on Saturday, with a federal warrant, and he will receive them in the library and offer them sherry.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To hear the right words on the radio at 8:40.

npcsInvolved.name: Frank Lusk, 49
npcsInvolved.description: At the viaduct at noon, at the back of the crowd. Whether he walks to the microphone is up to the party.

rewards.money: Sloane's $5,000 cheque, if the party took it (it bounces on Monday if he is dead or disgraced; Northgate's account is frozen by Hale if Hale is involved). Sloane's second $500, delivered on Saturday in an envelope, if he is alive to send it. A Ledger reward of $1,000 'for information leading to the truth about the Halvorsen fire', which Hollis Gage announces on Saturday and pays, eventually, in instalments. Teague's wallet ($200) and the $5,000 first half, if he is taken and the party is not honest with Hale.
items: The 1946 Lindqvist statement, original or carbon, and whatever the party chose to do with it
Teague's Colt .32 and the re-stamped twin (federal evidence if Hale has them)
Nora's unfired .32, if it was saved from the swap
A proof of the Courier's DA SLAIN page, whether or not it ran
Saturday's Ledger, whatever it says, framed on the agency wall
Award the 4,000 XP at the end of the night. The campaign tops out at 6th level; for players who carry these detectives on into another case, the XP counts toward 7th (23,000).

twists: Sloane's speechwriter put 'five years ago this very night' into the speech to mean five years since Sloane's first big trial, as a boast. Sloane did not notice. Teague did, from a copy of the speech Dunleavy got from Agnes Ruud's carbon, and timed his shot to it. A party that gets the speech changed (Agnes can retype it at 6 p.m.) takes away Teague's cue and Nora's moment at the same time.

If Sloane lives because the party saved him, he will try to destroy them. If he dies because they let him, Vantreight wins unless they have the evidence to beat him anyway. If he lives and the truth is printed, he is indicted in December for obstruction and conspiracy, loses on Tuesday by forty thousand votes, and is the most frightened man in the state prison by spring. The players should feel that saving him and punishing him are the same act.
Constance does not need rescuing. She needs one person to be kind to her for five minutes on a railway platform. That is the campaign's last scene if the party wants it to be.

Gil Maddox, the man with the bomb, is the only conspirator who ends the week in jail if the party does nothing. He tried to murder Sloane and is not innocent. He is also the only one who was honest about wanting to.

Vantreight's frame needs Nora to stand up. If she does not stand up, Teague still fires, and the frame fails, and Dunleavy has to improvise, and improvising in front of two thousand people is how lieutenants of police get caught.
dmTips: Run Act 3 in real time if the table can stand it. Say the minute aloud every round. The proscenium clock is two minutes slow; the players should feel the gap.

Have a written list of who is where at 8:35, and make the players commit their own positions before the scene starts. Then run the plan honestly. A good plan should work; a perfect plan should still have one surprise (the second route, the cut microphone, Constance standing up).

Teague is the deadliest single opponent in the campaign. The party is 6th level and has allies; he is CR 5 and alone, and he wants to escape, not to win. Use the full gunplay rules, cover (the box's front rail is half cover, the booth's tin walls are three-quarters), bystanders and noise. If he gets out of the alley door, he is gone unless Hale is watching the station.
Do not decide in advance whether Sloane lives. Decide in advance only what each NPC does, and let the dice and the plan do the rest.

The outcomes, for reference. Sloane: dead, wounded, or untouched. Nora: framed, cleared, or never in danger. The truth: printed in full, printed small, said on the radio, mailed to Miriam Holloway, or burned. Vantreight: indicted (needs Hale, the Hall of Records figures and Teague or the Courier proof), embarrassed (needs the Ledger), or untouched. Dunleavy: arrested, disgraced, or chief of police by Christmas. Each combination is a different city on Saturday morning; describe it.

Epilogue suggestions: Daniel Kessling is pardoned by the governor in April 1953, and Nora gets a byline at the Ledger. Mrs. Sorvik lights her candle on the new viaduct's lowest leg, where the city puts a small bronze plaque with eleven names. Frank Lusk resigns from Local 9 and goes back to the docks. Becerra makes lieutenant. Agnes Ruud retires. Teague is taken off the 11:15 at the state line, or is never seen again. Walt Embry pays the rent. The viaduct opens in 1953, and is ugly, and lasts sixty years.

Final headlines. Courier, Friday late edition: whichever page ran (if Sloane was shot and Nora arrested, DA SLAIN AT RALLY; if not, the HOLD page is melted down at midnight and the Courier runs SLOANE RALLY ENDS IN UPROAR). Ledger, Saturday: whatever the party earned. Read both aloud.
